Unit Outcomes
What you will learn
  • Use comparative forms to compare people, places, and ways of getting around
  • Describe transportation options and city routes
  • Write a formal letter of complaint with clear structure
  • Present facts and announce a decision in a discussion

Vocabulary
Advice on How to Get Around Your City
commute
to travel regularly between home and work or school
convenient
easy to use, suitable for your needs, saving time or effort
crowded
filled with more people than is comfortable
delay
a period of time when something happens later than expected
detour
a different route used when the main road is closed
fare
the money you pay to travel on public transportation
intersection
the place where two or more roads meet or cross
pedestrian
a person who is walking, especially near traffic
route
the way taken to get from one place to another
rush hour
the times of day when traffic is heaviest because people are traveling to or from work
schedule
a plan of times when buses, trains, or events will happen
traffic jam
a long line of vehicles that cannot move or move very slowly
transfer
to change from one bus, train, or route to another
subway
an underground railway system in a city

Grammar
Comparative Forms
Regular Comparatives
One-syllable adjectives: add -er
fast → faster
cheap → cheaper
large → larger
Two-syllable adjectives ending in -y: change y to i, add -er
heavy → heavier
early → earlier
busy → busier
Adjectives with two or more syllables: use more
expensive → more expensive
convenient → more convenient
comfortable → more comfortable
Irregular Comparatives
These adjectives do not follow normal rules.
good → better
bad → worse
far → farther / further
Using Comparisons
Use than to compare two things.
The subway is faster than the bus.
Walking is more relaxing than driving.
Use much / a lot / a little / even + comparative to emphasize.
The train is much faster than the car.
This route is a little more crowded.
Double comparative: The + comparative, the + comparative
The earlier you leave, the faster you arrive.
The more crowded the train, the more uncomfortable the ride.
Important: Do not use more with short adjectives that already take -er.

❌ The bus is more cheaper than the taxi.
✅ The bus is cheaper than the taxi.
Pronunciation: Stress in Comparative Adjectives

In one-syllable comparables, the stress stays on the same syllable: CHEAP → CHEAPer.

In longer comparatives with "more," the stress moves: conVENient → MORE conVENient.

Reading
One Foot on The Gas

🚗 One Foot on The Gas

For many children of immigrants in the United States, getting a driver's license is more than just a rite of passage — it is a bridge between two worlds. In One Foot on The Gas, journalist Maria Santos explores how second-generation Americans use cars to navigate both their parents' traditions and their own modern lives.

"My parents walked everywhere in their village in Guatemala," says Carlos Mendez, 22. "When they came to Los Angeles, they were afraid to drive. The freeways seemed dangerous, the traffic overwhelming. But for me, the car means freedom. I can go to work, to school, and to see friends without waiting for a bus that might be late."

Santos notes that this pattern repeats across the country. In cities with limited public transportation — like Houston, Phoenix, and Atlanta — owning a car is often necessary. But for families who have never owned a vehicle, the cost of buying, insuring, and maintaining a car can be a heavy burden. Some young people take on extra jobs just to afford their first used car, seeing it as an investment in their future.

The cultural impact goes deeper than convenience. For many, the car becomes a space where two cultures meet. Parents who do not speak English well can sit in the passenger seat while their children drive them to appointments. Music switches between Spanish-language radio and American hip-hop. Fast-food bags from two different worlds share the back seat.

However, the relationship with driving is not always positive. Traffic accidents are the leading cause of death for young people in the U.S., and inexperience plays a major role. Insurance costs for young drivers are much higher than for older drivers, creating another financial barrier. Environmental concerns also weigh on this generation, many of whom worry about carbon emissions and climate change.

"I love my car," says Aisha Patel, 19, whose parents emigrated from India. "But I also feel guilty. I know public transportation is better for the planet. If my city had a subway like New York or DC, I would use it. Until then, I am stuck with what I have."

Writing
Write a Letter of Complaint
Writing Strategy — Writing an Effective Letter of Complaint:
1. Greeting: Use Dear Sir/Madam or the person's name if you know it.
2. Introduction: State clearly why you are writing and what the problem is.
3. Details: Give specific facts — dates, times, locations, and what went wrong.
4. Expectations: Say clearly what you want the company to do (refund, apology, replacement).
5. Closing: End politely but firmly. Use Yours sincerely / Yours faithfully.

14 Park Avenue
Springfield, IL 62701
March 15, 2026

Customer Service Department
Metro Transit Authority
200 Central Plaza
Springfield, IL 62704

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to complain about the bus service on Route 42, which I use to commute to work every weekday morning.

For the past three weeks, the 7:30 a.m. bus has been consistently late — sometimes by as much as twenty minutes. Last Tuesday, March 10, the bus did not arrive at all, and I was forced to take a taxi, which cost me $28. As a result, I was late for an important meeting with my manager.

I have been a loyal customer for over two years, and I have never experienced problems like this before. I understand that traffic can be unpredictable, but the delays have become too frequent to ignore.

I would like to request a full refund for the taxi fare and an assurance that the schedule will be improved. I have attached a copy of my taxi receipt for your records.

I look forward to hearing from you within the next ten days.

Yours faithfully,
Jordan Lee

Speaking
Consider the Facts in an Immigration Case
Exercise A — Presenting Facts and Announcing a Decision

Read the case below. Work in a group. Each person presents one fact. Then the group makes a decision together.

The Case: Maria's Commute

Maria is an immigrant who works as a nurse at a hospital 25 miles from her home. She does not have a car. The bus route to the hospital was cancelled last month. The new route requires two transfers and takes two hours each way. A community group has offered to start a van service, but they need permission from the city. Should the city approve the van service?

1. How important is reliable transportation for workers?
2. Should the city pay for transportation for all workers?
3. Is a private van service better than no service at all?
Speaking Strategy — Presenting Facts and Announcing a Decision:

Presenting facts: "The evidence shows that..." / "According to the report..." / "One important fact is..." / "We know that..."
Announcing a decision: "After considering all the facts, we have decided to..." / "The committee agrees that..." / "Our final decision is..."
Roleplay: City Council Meeting

Student A (City Council Member): You must decide whether to approve the van service. Ask for facts about cost, safety, and number of people who will use it. Listen carefully and then announce your decision.

Student B (Community Group Representative): You want the van service approved. Present facts about how many people need it, how much it will cost, and why it is safer than the current situation. Use comparatives.

Student C (Hospital Manager): You need Maria and other nurses to arrive on time. Explain what happens when staff are late. Give facts about patient care.
